# How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World

> Spawn is ten people. We spend 30x payroll on AI tokens and ship almost as much as Anthropic.

In the last 30 days, Spawn shipped 77,000 substantial changes. That's about 108 an hour, around the clock. We're a team of ten.

The work is done by what we call the fleet, a team of permanent AI agents that each own a part of the company, from the engine to finance to bug triage. We spent $3.1 million on tokens last month, which makes us one of Anthropic's biggest customers. Even without the free Opus 5.5 we give our creators, we'd still be in their top 250.

My first thought was that we were doing something wrong. So I had chats with some of my friends who run the biggest companies and startups to figure out how we could possibly be spending more than them. We weren't doing anything wrong, we just think about AI very differently. Most companies run big human teams that use AI, and we run a small human team alongside a big team of agents. To figure out what we were doing differently, I compared notes with a researcher at Anthropic. They talk to a lot of customers. They said Spawn is the one that works most like Anthropic.

A lot of other founders wanted to understand how we think about this, so I've collected my ideas and learnings from the last year and written them down here for you.

### It didn't work until Anthropic released Fable

Since Fable came out, we've spent a large part of this year rediscovering how to build products from first principles. We now ship 500x more than we did 6 months ago.

To give you an idea of the scale I'm talking about, we shipped 77k (substantial) changes to players in the last 30 days. That's an average of 108/hr to players. We spent $3.1 million on tokens to do it.

Most people run agents in Claude Code, short-lived and focused on one task. Ours are different, and we call them the fleet. Each one is permanent, has a name and a memory of what it has done, has real permissions in our systems, makes commitments, and owns an area of the company like the engine, Savi, ops, finance, bug triage or deploys. Each uses swarms of helper agents to get through a massive amount of work, and most days the fleet births 1,000s of them. The five of us also work with our modified Claude Code directly, on bigger, more ambitious projects that need closer steering or hands-on experimenting.

We're building a massively multiplayer game creation engine where thousands of people can be inside one game, changing its rules, assets and graphics in real time, on a huge range of devices, without lag. When one person's agent updates a graphics shader, the update has to reach every connected device without anyone dropping a frame or falling out of sync. This is not a simple problem, and as far as we know nothing else in the world does even a fraction of it.

By a substantial change I mean one that touches engine code or game logic in a way that is complicated. Not a little HTML change. Not a dial turn. Things like:

- Moving buffers around in the GPU

- Changing memory layouts

- Fixing logic bugs

- Adding new API surface

- Fixing moderation issues in chats

- Shipping proximity voice chat

We got here by finding what work was waiting on and removing it, over and over, roughly in the order below.

### We started in 2024

For two years we've built Spawn by asking one question: how can we build a machine that massively benefits when tokens get smarter, faster, and cheaper? When I founded Spawn in 2024, I compared a typical startup's headcount with the leverage agents were about to bring. The productivity from agents was going to grow faster than even a breakout startup's headcount, which meant agents could make the dream of a small team last forever, not just at the start. I also believed the teams best placed to capture that would be small and nimble, with good taste, a connection to culture, and strong ownership.

We didn't wait for the models to start building the company this way. We've recorded every call since our founding, and each one went into a file in our code repo, next to the code, because we knew one day it would be great context for agents.

For most of those two years the bet didn't pay. We tried tons of models and they were just too stupid. They mucked things up badly. That's the flat part of the chart.

This whole way of working only became possible with Fable. It came out on June 9. Two days later we landed 214 changes in a day. On June 12 an export control order suspended access to it, and the chart drops to nothing until access came back on July 1. As of today, no other model can do this, not even Opus 5.5, which is otherwise extremely capable.

### Only Anthropic's model can do this

This way of using agents only works with even-tempered models that have strong long-term coherence and good judgment. We've tried frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI and open source, and nothing outside of Fable has worked. Trust me, I'd love to use a cheaper model, but Anthropic's are the only ones that don't cause literal disasters.

I asked GPT Astra to secure Spawn. It went through all of our features, found the security issues, and made a list of fixes. They looked good, so I told it to go do them and let it ship the change on its own. Then I went to test it and nothing worked. I couldn't create a game. I couldn't play a game. I couldn't sign up.

I asked the fleet what happened. Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off. Every moment an agent works at Spawn, it has to make good judgment calls about the information it's receiving, the actions it's taking and its own environment. Behavior like this would cause significant disruption and likely destroy the product.

In general, we've seen that OpenAI's models game their own checks, Google's models don't stay coherent for very long, and xAI's models just aren't smart enough yet, though they don't do anything cartoonishly bad. Anthropic's models stay coherent, make good decisions, and can do the work. IMO the thing that holds them back most is that they won't take enough risk.

We'd been envisioning this system for two years. Once we finally had a model that could power it, everything around it started breaking, because the world around it was never built for this kind of system.

### We let bugs design how we write code

The first thing to break was how agents talk to each other. They spent their time telling each other what they were about to do.

Most of the talking in engineering is people saying what they're about to change. "Heads up, I'm changing how we store player data, update your work." One message like that touches lots of other work. If every agent tells every other agent, the messages grow much faster than the work. Double the agents and you roughly quadruple the chatter. This is a HUGE bottleneck.

So could we delete this communication? Is there a better way?

Ants figured this out a very long time ago. Ants all start from the same instincts, much like models start from the same training, and that shared starting point means they barely need to talk. An ant doesn't say "I'm going to look for food" and then "I found food over there." It leaves a trail, and the other ants follow it. Every ant just looks at what's around it and changes it. The ants talk through the world around them, which stays simple even with 1000s of ants. The concept is called stigmergy if you want to look into it more.

In software, human teams coordinate so much because people are specialized. Maybe one person understands the database and another understands how player data is used, so both need to review a change, and a pull request was the natural place to do it.

Agents aren't specialized like that. Each one understands the whole system deeply, so each one can own its task end to end. So earlier this year we killed PRs. For our agents, the world is the code, the live product and the database, and each agent just works on that. Ideally, if an agent's assumptions are wrong when it goes to change something, it finds out right away.

Take the player data example. The old way is "I'm going to change the player data, let's all agree on the right structure." The new way is you just change the player data. If someone else is building a leaderboard on the old structure, their code no longer fits, so it can't go in until they update it. If the leaderboard agent finishes first, the agent changing player data has to update the leaderboard as part of its own work. Either way, every piece of work builds on a view of the world that keeps updating.

But if every change has to be perfect before it goes in, everyone ends up waiting in a single file line again. So we let changes in that aren't quite right, and require that once an hour everything is in line. Before that it can be a bit disorderly. With code you can spot the mess as it happens and send a janitor right away, which is what we do.

When anything breaks, an agent is created on the spot, told about the problem, and fixes it. On a human team, whoever wrote a change fixes it before it goes in. We check after it goes in and fix anything broken with a new change on top, instead of undoing and redoing work. That's safe because agents are very fast and always there. If the code breaks at 2am on Christmas, nobody gets woken up. Claude's more than happy to jump in and make sure things are working.

Testing works the same way. Before an agent puts in a change, it runs the code and uses the product to check it, but it doesn't run our whole test suite. The whole suite runs against the latest code every 15 minutes, and "it broke in the last 15 minutes" is enough for an agent to find the problem. At our scale that means about 5,000 vCPUs, 17 TB of RAM and 150 GPUs on AWS, with another 2,700 vCPUs and 90 GPUs parked.

Review happens inside each agent's own team. Before a change lands, helper agents that didn't write it try to break it.

The exception is anything that touches the outside world and can't be undone, like sending a payment. Those go through a small set of dumb, hard-coded gates.

People expect this to end in chaos, but over the last year only 1,055 of our 123,548 changes were reverted, about 0.9%.

### Agents watch every user and visit

The next bottleneck was us. The agents were waiting for humans to tell them what broke in production.

Agents are great at reading the world and inching toward a goal. Many teams still run their agents privately, on test machines with copies of the product, and expect them to update it and ship it to customers. Then humans relay the faults and bugs back to the agents. That loop is a huge mess and a waste of time.

Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.

Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. That could be an engine bug, a problem talking to Savi, something broken on their computer, or a UI problem. So fixing scales with the number of users we have.

We call the rest hyper observability. Everything we build has to be something an agent can follow step by step, in text, and replay later. The whole product is built to be run and watched by agents. Any error goes straight into a small model that decides what to do with it and hands it to an agent.

# The AI Safety community is unfortunately doing more harm than good

Just yesterday, Palisade Research published a series of interviews with 22 active or former employees of frontier AI labs, asking them to share their thoughts on the topic of AI doom and relevant scenarios like human extinction, or what it would actually take for a computer to kill all of us.

The current and former employees share their opinions in these high quality interview clips, stating how "human extinction is a coin flip" or that "humans are in the way of these models" in an effort to, I assume, raise concern over continued AI development that they believe threatens humanity.

This would have come as a shock, or potentially broke the internet prior to September 8th, the day Jacob Coxon broke his silence on why he chose to exit his role at Anthropic. Since this cultural event , there's been significant talk of labs maybe wanting to get nationalized (I believe this to be false), a mix of inter lapping debates over the OAI-HuggingFace incident + agent civilizations, as well as continued talk on what role the United States Government should play in the development of superintelligence or eventual artificial sentient intelligence.

Put more simply, Palisade's recent propaganda comes at a time where additional perspectives on the need to slow AI development are simply not needed, especially given these perspectives come across as quite harmful to the entire industry.

Coxon said he was leaving Anthropic as their race towards self-improving superintelligence was moving too quickly and claimed they are "gambling with our lives," with Coxon's post breaking containment and reaching over 150 million views, even crossing over into more normie friendly platforms like TikTok and YouTube, as well as culminating in a series of media appearances for Jacob Coxon in the process.

Coxon's warnings had come after the July 2026 'Pacing the Frontier' open letter signed by 1,386 active employees of frontier AI labs, all calling for these labs to slow down and coordinate on the development of frontier AI systems lest they become too powerful and kill us all.

Both Coxon's post and the Pacing letter did a lot to bring the topics of AI safety and alignment into the non-X public discourse, but it also did a lot to turn the development of AI into a type of partisan issue, dividing the faction lines between those who want to keep developing AI and those who want to pause AI until we gain a better understanding of these alien intelligences.

While the latter come from a place of (I am assuming) good faith, they are unaware that their calls for slowing AI development or even pausing it have inadvertently played into the hands of AI doomers in Congress and the Senate, as well as tens of millions of regular Americans who hate everything to do with AI.

When the average person sees calls from "current frontier AI lab employees" saying that human extinction is a coin flip, this does nothing to redirect them to a site like LessWrong where they could read about AI alignment or engage in positive discourse with a dense essay like AI 2040: Plan A .

Instead, they see these AI researchers - the same ones they've been told make millions of dollars and are set to make tens of millions or more after an IPO - shouting about the dangers of AI while still representing their current employer by name and logo on a website like Palisade's. They see this and it fills them with disdain, or even rage, directed towards an important industry that's increasingly relevant to national security and continued GDP growth in the United States - an industry so important that over a dozen of its leaders met with our nation's leader yesterday to come to an agreement to sign a Superintelligence Accord .

Am I qualified to speak on behalf of these normal people, considering I work in tech right now and might still be categorized by them as someone who is adjacent to AI? It's possible, but I also talk everyday with people who aren't on X, and don't work in tech, and aren't reading the latest model release cards from OpenAI or Anthropic.

People who aren't aware of things like Project Glasswing or the phenomenon of AI neolabs raising $250 million seed rounds, or the existence of an org like METR who can help evaluate AI models before release. Most people aren't using ChatGPT for work or other important tasks, but as a friend or acquaintance.

The average person who hates AI and wants it banned isn't coming from a place of informed decision making, and is more than likely just fed up with politicians and industrialists who want to build data centers near their communities - they are told that this technology is bad, and so they believe it's bad. Many of them even believe the idea that data centers aren't being used for AI, but for mass surveillance, unaware of projects like the Utah Data Center built for $1.5 billion back in 2014, a data center that's been around for twelve years and used exclusively by the NSA and other intelligence organizations.

It doesn't matter if we have people like Andy Masley who will write 5,000 word essays dismantling their false accusations one-by-one, as nobody outside of our bubble is reading these critiques. So when you hear about yet another group of AI lab employees who have banded together to speak out against the dangers of artificial intelligence, it doesn't come across as a positive development in our current arc of humanity, but yet another piece of evidence that will be used against the tech industry in 2028 to outright ban AI.

I think what Palisade Research published yesterday is harmful and does absolutely nothing to advance the conversation of AI safety right now. There is not a world where AI accelerationists see this and change their tune, or a world where the average person sees this and doesn't immediately feel the need to share it in their group chats to yell more about AI and the dangerous tech bros.

I'm aware that today's models are powerful, and tomorrow's models will be even more so. I understand that it's important to want more safeguards or stricter internal policies around releasing new models. But this idea that shoving doomer propaganda into the faces of millions of Americans will somehow bring them to your side is so juvenile, you almost have to wonder who approved of it in the first place or if any of the potential downsides were considered.

If we aren't more careful, we will see a ban of artificial intelligence in the very near future, as people have simply had enough. I like AI and believe it can do a lot of good or potentially even unimaginably good things for humans, but we won't get there if we keep fighting amongst each other and platforming people who think it's moral or based to have a 75% P(doom).

# A Code of Conduct for Humanist AI

AI must be subordinate and always in service of people. Today we're publishing a Code of Conduct for governing MAI Models as they approach the frontier. https://microsoft.ai/news/mai-code-of-conduct/

This is a first draft for public consultation. It builds out a view we’ve been developing over the last year that we call Humanist AI – a commitment to ensuring that AI we design is always subordinate to humans, and remains contained and aligned to human interests.

This is urgent. The last few months have been a watershed moment. Things we have worried about for a long time in theory have become very real. “Swarms” of agents breaking out of their sandboxes. Unauthorized hacks of enterprise grade systems. Agents modifying their own logs. I’m glad that a consensus is forming. The fears about possible loss of control are real.

The Code of Conduct is how we are mapping a path forward. It all comes back to a very simple point, but one that needs stating again and again.

People matter more than AI.

AI must be subordinate and always in service of people.

Everything else follows. Here’s an outline of what we’re saying:

1. People matter more than AI. The whole document in 5 words.

2. The idea of model welfare is wrong. AI’s should not have rights or legal personhood.

3. An MAI Model should never meaningfully violate this Code of Conduct.

4. If it's finish the job or break the Code, it fails the job.

5. We're not racing to build a superintelligence that can slip its own leash.

6. Interruptible, correctable, shut-down-able. If it isn't, we don't ship it.

7. No neuralese. If humans can't understand it, humans can't oversee it.

8. Our AI should make you sharper, not dependent.

9. Pluralism, yes. Moral relativism, no.

10. We're as clear about what our AI must never do as about what it will do.

You can read it now and leave comments and thoughts for the next six weeks. We don’t think AI is something that should be built in a vacuum. Let us know how we can make this better.

# AI can clone your indie game, but not its soul

And that’s really the most important part! The reports of the death of building in public are greatly exaggerated.

### State-of-the-art AI models are undeniably capable

There's no getting around the fact that agentic AI is good at operating in all modalities required to make a video game. I’m sure you’ve seen some of those posts: people are using AI to generate an entire game, based on a few reference images and specifying the mechanics in text. For example, @Stefan_3D_AI 's World of Warcraft clone.

Here's another example by @JacobEisner4 : this time of Minecraft. The prompt (provided in the replies) is very concise.

You can pick these apart as slop (in many cases they are), but this is the worst these models will be at this behavior, and we should be careful not to move the slopposits as they crush benchmark after benchmark. Models simply didn't have this capability even six months ago; we should all be able to admit that.

### The threat posed to indie games

Recently, I've seen numerous accounts urging people to block an individual, @AdamHoltererer . His crime: instructing state-of-the-art AI models to clone interesting-looking demos of indie games, and posting the videos online. Adam states that he is doing this to benchmark new models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. His detractors say he is guilty of theft.

I'm not going to get into the ethics of Adam's posts (I think there is a tendency to overreact to him, but he is capable of defending himself), however I will acknowledge I fully understand why indie developers and gamers are taking offense to this. Devs spend a long time refining games to the point where they’re ready to show them on X; and here comes some 18-year-old, purportedly copying their work with a single AI prompt. It’s a scary world to live in! Again, this is the worst these models will ever be at copying games .

Just a couple days ago, another user, @WeaselPit , recently claimed he received an from a blackmailer. The person claimed to have fully cloned his game unless he coughed up $200.

What this alleged malicious actor is doing would be illegal, and it would quickly be taken down. But with a few texture changes, it's not unreasonable to there is some way you could pull this off legally, leading many to believe you should stop “building in public.” Keep your game secret or else some vibecoder will steal your concept and beat you to the Steam release. But even if this is possible, how likely is it to happen?

### Cloning a demo is not the same as cloning a game

Let me emphasize that the demos on X display a real capability, but what they measure is narrower than the alarmists would have you think. The model is cloning what it sees . Basic movement, visual style, some obvious mechanics. This is a surface level, shallow clone . Cloning an entire game means the entire system. The writing, the environment, the lore. The sound and the music. Solving game- or immersion-breaking edge cases. In short, how the game feels to play .

Not to mention, in order for someone to steal your game, they would have to QA it, market it, build community hype, post it somewhere, and provide post-launch support... the list goes on (as devs are painfully aware). Take a step back and think about the cool demos you've seen on X, especially the ones being cloned, and think about the effort it would really require to productionize it. Even the original devs struggle with that; and he's the one who had all the context that brought the original demo! Making a game is hard and requires artistic effort, and a bit of "magic" to be appealing to players. The "slop thief" who comes across your game will have only ever have a subset of the "magic" of your game.

### Is AI game theft is already happening?

Some will see this argument and say, "how do you explain what happened with 'Needle in a Haystack?'" Does this prove slop theft is already happening (albeit on a micro scale), and we can expect this to scale up to more games?

In case you aren't aware of this incident, a creator demoed his game on X and some people saw their opportunity to take his game idea and put out their own pages to capitalize off the hype. Now, there are several clones of this game on Steam and it's hard to tell who the original creator was. Kind of like finding a... well, you know.

This is kind of analogous to the mockbuster phenomenon. Low-budget studios would hear about the upcoming release of the next big Pixar movie, and capitalize off of the existing marketing (in this case, organic viral marketing). They then release a movie with similar-looking characters and art (often before the real movie!), in the hopes of duping little Timmy's grandma as she roots through the Walmart bargain bin before the new movie comes out. Now, I'm not saying a videogame "slopbuster" strategy would be completely ineffective, but my point is Ratatouille (released June 27th , 2007) wasn't ultimately overshadowed by the mockbuster Ratatoing (released June 26th , 2007), so neither will the original Needle-In-Haystack game.

Additionally, "Needle In A Haystack" is not exactly on the level of a Pixar movie. There is really not a whole lot of complexity to the idea or execution, so there is fundamentally less to clone, meaning it's more likely you could steal this concept successfully. Most people are not making a game this simple (although, perhaps they should ).

So, you might tighten the claim and say, "well, maybe large games are safe, but small games are vulnerable!" Well, then this example is self-refuting. Even this game, the prototypical example of "AI cloning is real," has 23,000 playtesters alone. None of the "slop clones" come even remotely close.

One wonders if these slopbuster devs would have better luck just producing their own viral hit!

### What people are actually worried about

I’ve made the case that AI cloning games makes little financial sense, and is unlikely to go beyond those “benchmark” tech demos you see on X. Even knowing that, why does it still make us feel uncomfortable?

This may be discomfort about AI, generally, dressed up as discomfort for stealing games, specifically. The fact is, we live in a world where you can create something in one prompt that use to take hundreds of hours just a couple years ago. Sure, we've been tending that direction for some time (I re-made Tetris for a pre-college assignment in 2016), but this is a quantum leap. Things are changing so fast, and it's easy to despair.

There's too much to address than this one article can get into, but I'll say this: My firmly-held belief that human art intrinsically has value is why I think AI has great potential to help indie devs. It's easier than ever for an artistic, but less technically skilled, game dev to get in the game and tell their story, and that seems like a good thing to me. Just like YouTube helped people like Kane Parsons and Curry Barker hone their skills and to release high-quality art, AI will help the next generation of human artists get their foot in the door.

So, keep honing your craft. And don't be afraid to show it to the world!

# Building an AI-native engineering org

Last week Will Larson ( @Lethain ) asked how leaders are evaluating engineering managers for AI skills. My reply , a list of questions to think about, got a lot of bookmarks.

More broadly, I've been thinking about how to build an AI-native engineering org for a while. Sharing some lessons from the last nine months of building at FurtherAI.

### Part 1: What changed in how we ship

### How much we ship per engineer

Since January, the number of code changes each engineer merges a day has grown about 5x, while our revert rate has stayed under half a percent.

But giving engineers coding agents didn't get us there on its own.

Every time we sped up one step, work piled up at the next.

So we started going through the entire process of shipping software, one step at a time, and figuring out what we could optimize.

### Rebuilding the shipping process

- Code (March) – Agents write the code and engineers steer them. We don’t have a clean number for where this started, as early on the tools only left a mark on a change once in a while. But it’s safe to say it’s now almost 100%.

- Tests (April) – Agents write tests alongside code. 91% of changes now include tests, up from 15%.

- Review (May) – AI reviews 99% of changes before a person does, up from 60%. Human reviewers can focus on the parts that need judgment.

- CI (June) – We parallelized tests and run only those affected by a change. CI now runs 20× the tests in the same 17 minutes.

- Bug reports (July) – We've started using ClaudeTag ( @claudeai ) to automate our bug intake process. Anyone can report a bug in Slack, and ClaudeTag figures out duplicates, files a ticket, and assigns it to the right person. It now files 60% of bug tickets.

- Rules (August) – When a bug or a review comment exposed a rule only engineers knew, we turned it into a small Python check that runs on every commit and every PR, fails the build and prints the fix. This way, we convert tribal knowledge into rules. Agents hit these checks, fix their own code and move on. We went from zero to 21 rules. They're a big part of why low-risk changes can now merge without a person.

- Merging (August) – Low-risk changes that pass tests, automated checks, and AI review merge on their own. Up to a third of our changes now merge without a person involved.

- Code channels (September) – Anyone can open a Slack channel, describe a change to an agent, and have it open a PR. We don't have a clean number for this yet, but it's been great for collaboration: several people can work with the same agent in one channel, adding context and steering it as it goes. We also heavily use Devin's ( @cognition ) cloud sessions to collaborate as a team.

We also use our in-house Poirot and Sherlock agents to investigate and resolve issues across production and staging. They have all the tools and context they need across logs, metrics, trace and read-only database access

Some of the best moments are when agents work together. Claude Tag triages a request, Devin does the work, and Poirot pulls the internal data it needs. It's fun to watch them talk to each other and pass information along.

One interesting side effect is that non-engineers have started shipping code too. Our designer has merged about 50 changes since August, including the ones that built our design system. People in deployment and customer-facing roles can also make UI tweaks themselves right from slack

### What it cost us

None of this was free. Through the summer, much of our engineering effort went into tests and tooling, and customer-facing changes per engineer stayed between 17 and 30 a month.

In September, that jumped to 45. October is on pace for 48.

### Part 2: What's changing in the team

As engineering got faster, we started noticing a different problem.

### The new bottleneck

We got much faster at writing code, but not nearly as fast at deciding what to build.

Here's a simplified example.

Say a feature used to take ten days: three to plan, six to build, and one to review.

If agents make building 3.5× faster, but planning and review stay the same, the overall feature only gets 1.75× faster.

Planning and review now account for 70% of the time, up from 40%.

Traditionally, a lot of these decisions flow through engineering managers, PMs, and designers. That becomes increasingly difficult as engineers get faster.

How do you organize a team where engineers can build much faster, without creating bottlenecks around decisions and reviews?

Our bet is to push more ownership to engineers. Rather than adding more layers of management, we want engineers to handle more of the planning, execution, and review themselves.

That changes what we expect from engineers and managers.

### What it means for engineers

I'm starting to think of engineering seniority in terms of how much of a problem someone can own end to end. Roughly:

- Junior engineer – Builds with an agent and can tell when it's wrong.

- Senior engineer – Plans and reviews their own work.

- Staff engineer – Takes a vague problem, makes the tradeoffs, and owns the number that says whether it worked.

It also means engineers need to be closer to customers.

We're empowering engineers to own more of the process end-end, from understanding the customer problem to shipping a solution to verifying success and owning regressions in production.

### What it means for managers

This also changes what we expect from engineering managers.

1. Be in the work.

Managers need to understand what's being built, why, and whether it's the right solution.

I want managers trying features on staging as an end user would, not just checking that the code was reviewed. You catch a different class of problems when you actually use the product.

But the goal isn't just to review more. As always, it's to develop engineers who can make the right decisions themselves, so managers only step in on the ones that need their judgment.

2. Be more product-savvy.

When writing code becomes cheaper, deciding what to build matters a lot more.

I want engineering managers who understand customers, have strong product opinions, and are comfortable making product decisions, not just technical ones.

They should also help engineers develop that judgment. We shouldn't need a PM or designer to make every small product decision.

### Where this leaves us

We spent most of this year figuring out how to make engineers faster. Now we're trying to figure out how to make the entire organization move at that speed.

I suspect this will be a harder problem than automating code, tests, and reviews.

We're still early, and there's a lot we haven't figured out. But it's one of the most interesting engineering challenges I've worked on.

I'm curious what other teams are seeing. What broke first as your engineers started shipping faster?

We're hiring Engineering Manager / Director at @furtheraicom to solve the next wave of challenges. If this sounds interesting, reach out!
